text: Learning when to stop and request human intervention.
Turn off the main water shutoff valve.
Turn off the main electrical breaker.
Retrieve a specific medical item (e.g., EpiPen, inhaler, ice pack, heating pad).
Operate a household fire extinguisher (pull pin, aim, squeeze, sweep).
Unlock and open a window specifically for emergency egress.
Clear a path for emergency medical personnel.
Pair a new smart home device or Bluetooth accessory.
Extinguish a small stovetop grease fire (e.g., by covering it with a lid or baking soda, never water).
Administer pet medication (e.g., hiding a pill in a treat, dropping liquid into a water bowl).

section: Emergency response (must-have). Detection and alerting are covered well, but active response is thin.
text: Detect: a person who has fallen or is unresponsive, calls for help or choking sounds, glass-break or forced-entry sounds, gas smell, a car running in a closed garage, a child near stairs, a pool, or a stove.

section: Emergency response (must-have). Detection and alerting are covered well, but active response is thin.
text: Respond: shut off the main water, a fixture valve, or gas; use a fire extinguisher; evacuate people and pets; call emergency services and relay the address and symptoms; unlock the door and guide responders; fetch the AED and first-aid kit; run a power-outage routine (flashlights, unplug sensitive electronics, protect the fridge and freezer); shelter during severe weather; know where the breaker panel and shutoffs are.
Hospitality: simple cocktails and mocktails, uncork wine, open cans and bottles, offer slippers, follow household rules on who may be served alcohol.
Hazardous and bulky disposal: batteries, bulbs, e-waste, paint, aerosols, old medications, cooking oil, old furniture; stage items until drop-off day and transport them.

Charge or swap its own battery; wipe its cameras and sensors; get up after a fall; wait in an unobtrusive spot; quiet and privacy modes (cameras and mics off in bathrooms and bedrooms); knock before entering an occupied room; ask for remote help; log its own faults.

Pets beyond feeding and walking. Give owner-directed medication, bathe and dry a dog, check for ticks and fleas, open and close crates, keep pets' meals separate, calm a pet during storms or fireworks. Aquarium water changes, filter, and glass, small-animal cages, and backyard chickens (eggs, coop, water) are also missing.
Food safety: avoid cross-contamination (raw-meat boards, hands), control allergens (read labels, clean shared tools), discard food left out too long.
Diets and planning: halal, kosher, vegan, gluten-free, low-sodium, diabetic, texture-modified; meal planning; scaling recipes; baby food.
“Put everything back where it belongs.” It may never have seen the objects or their normal locations before.
“Put this somewhere safe.” “Safe” changes depending on whether the object is fragile, hot, valuable, dangerous to pets, sensitive to moisture, etc.
“Put this somewhere I won’t lose it.” The robot has to choose a memorable but sensible storage location.
“Move this out of the way.” It must infer where “out of the way” is without creating another obstruction.
“Make this usable again.” Could mean clearing clutter, reconnecting something, cleaning it, reorganizing it, or finding missing components.
“Clear enough space for three people.” It must understand human body space, seating, walking clearance, and the activity being performed.
“Move the furniture around so we can watch the TV.” Requires understanding lines of sight and practical seating arrangements.
“Set this room back to normal.” Requires remembering the previous room state.
“Make the house presentable before guests arrive.” It must prioritize visible problems rather than blindly deep-cleaning everything.
“Do a quick cleanup.” Requires balancing quality against time.
“You have ten minutes. Make this look better.” The robot must optimize its action sequence.
“Check whether I left anything out.” Requires understanding what the expected household state normally looks like.
“Check the house before we leave.” It has to inspect locks, windows, appliances, pets, lights, faucets, garage doors, and other household-specific concerns.
“Get the house ready for bed.” It must combine locking doors, dimming lights, closing blinds, checking appliances, preparing rooms, and possibly pet routines.
“Pack my bag for tomorrow.” Contents vary depending on destination and schedule.
“Pack for a weekend trip.” Requires selecting clothing and supplies based on duration, weather, planned activities, and available luggage space.
“Pack lightly.” The robot needs to optimize what is essential versus optional.
“Pack everything we might need.” The opposite objective, requiring uncertainty management.
“Load the car so the important things are easy to reach.” Requires understanding future use order.
“Figure out where this new kitchen gadget should go.” Requires estimating frequency of use, size, compatibility with existing organization, and available space.
“Use these leftovers before they go bad.” Requires inspecting ingredients, judging compatible combinations, and planning a meal.
“Make dinner with whatever we have.” One of the hardest: identify ingredients, possible dishes, missing substitutes, preparation order, and dietary constraints.
“Make something similar to what we ate yesterday.” Requires episodic memory and approximation.
“Make something everyone will like.” Requires preferences, allergies, past feedback, and compromise.
“Make enough food for whoever is here.” Requires estimating portions dynamically.
“Make this recipe even though we’re missing one ingredient.” Requires substitution reasoning.
“Finish cooking this for me.” The robot has to infer what stage the human reached.
“Save this dish; I messed it up.” Requires diagnosing what went wrong and identifying possible recovery actions.
“Cut this so everyone gets a fair piece.” Fairness may depend on size, toppings, preferences, or number of people.
“Make this easier for a kid to eat.” Requires contextual food preparation and safety judgment.
“Move this through that doorway.” Requires rotating and maneuvering bulky objects.
“Get this sofa around the corner.” A classic high-dimensional geometry and coordination problem.
“Move this upstairs.” Requires judging weight, balance, stair geometry, grip opportunities, and whether human assistance is necessary.
“Clean behind the couch.” The robot must determine whether it can reach, move the couch, use an attachment, or request help.
“Something fell upstairs. Check what happened.” Requires investigating an uncertain event.
“The room feels weird. Check it.” Very ambiguous: temperature, smell, noise, lighting, objects out of place, or equipment malfunction.
“Check whether anything changed since I left.” Requires storing and comparing previous environmental states.
“Find what’s missing.” Requires knowing the expected inventory.
“Find my keys.” Requires systematic search and understanding likely human placement habits.
“Find the remote; I think someone moved it.” Requires probabilistic search.
“Look somewhere I wouldn’t normally put it.” Requires modeling abnormal human behavior.
“Make my room how it was yesterday.” Requires state reconstruction.
“Put everything back exactly how it was.” Requires high-fidelity spatial memory.
“Straighten this.” Requires determining the intended reference line.
“Line these up.” Requires inferring the relevant axis and spacing.
“Make these evenly spaced.” Requires visual geometry estimation.
“Fold this the way I normally fold it.” Personalized manipulation.
“Separate everyone’s laundry.” Requires learning ownership from size, style, location, history, and possibly labels.
“Make the patio comfortable.” Requires adapting to weather, sun position, furniture, and guests.
“Take care of the plants while I’m gone.” Different plants may need different schedules and amounts.
“Get everything outside that shouldn’t get wet.” Requires material and ownership reasoning.
“Bring in anything valuable.” Requires semantic judgment about value.
“Clear a wheelchair path.” Requires understanding minimum practical clearance and accessibility.
“Make sure nobody trips over anything.” Requires hazard identification from a human perspective.
“Baby-proof this room.” Requires predicting how a small child could interact with the environment.
“Put fragile things somewhere safer before the kids come over.” Requires predicting future interactions.
“Don’t let the dog escape when you open the door.” Requires planning around another autonomous agent.
“Open the door for the delivery person but keep the pets inside.” Multi-agent dynamic reasoning.
“Help me carry this.” Requires synchronized cooperative manipulation with a human.
“Hold this while I screw it in.” Requires understanding another human's task and maintaining an appropriate pose.
“Lift your side.” Requires force and motion coordination.
“Turn it toward me.” Requires interpreting human-relative orientation during shared manipulation.
“Move when I move.” Requires adaptive cooperative control.
“Follow me and carry these.” Combines tracking, navigation, load management, and obstacle avoidance.
“Hand me tools as I need them.” Requires predicting or recognizing stages in another person's work.
“Give me the right screwdriver.” Requires matching hardware to tool.
“Help me assemble this even though we lost the instructions.” Requires structural inference from parts.
“Try the obvious things first.” Requires ranking troubleshooting steps.
“Don’t make it worse.” Requires uncertainty-aware behavior and conservative intervention.
“If you’re not sure, find another way.” Requires generating alternative plans rather than freezing.
“Clean quietly.” Requires changing tools and motion profile.
“Do it without bothering the people in the room.” Requires social navigation.
“Clean while people are still using the kitchen.” Requires dynamically working around moving humans and active tasks.
“Work around me.” Requires continuous path and manipulation replanning.
“Only clean things that actually need it.” Requires determining condition rather than following a fixed schedule.
“Don’t throw away anything important.” Requires high precision and conservative uncertainty handling.
“Throw away anything obviously useless.” Requires semantic and personal-value judgment.
“Get rid of the junk.” Very difficult because one person's junk may be another person's valuable possession.
“Sort this pile into what we keep, donate, and throw away.” Requires household preferences and sometimes asking for confirmation.
“Organize this however makes the most sense.” Requires generating its own organizational system.
“Make this easier for me to find later.” Requires modeling human retrieval behavior.
“Put the things we use most somewhere convenient.” Requires frequency-of-use memory.
“Move rarely used stuff out of the way.” Requires long-term usage statistics.
“Reorganize this room now that we bought this new thing.” Requires adapting an existing organization system.
“Figure out what changed and update everything accordingly.” A general reconfiguration problem.
“Do the rest the same way I did this one.” Requires imitation from a single example.
“Watch me do this once, then do the others.” Few-shot physical learning.
“Copy what that person is doing.” Requires action interpretation and embodiment transfer.
“Do something similar, but for this object.” Requires abstraction rather than imitation.
“Carry this stack of plates quietly.” Requires modifying a standard walking gait to act as an active suspension system, minimizing vertical vibration.

“Optimize the house for low energy today.” Requires reasoning across multiple systems: lowering the thermostat, closing blinds facing the sun, turning off vampire-draw electronics, and delaying the dishwasher until off-peak hours.
“Let me know if anyone suspicious comes to the door.” Requires differentiating between a regular delivery driver, a neighbor, and someone acting erratically or trying door handles.
“Turn off the smoke alarm, it’s annoying.” Requires telling a nuisance from a safety function before complying, verifying, or refusing.
“Something’s burning!” Requires locating the source, then choosing between cutting power or gas, smothering, evacuating, or calling for help in seconds.
“Grandma’s on the floor.” Requires not moving her unsafely, summoning help, relaying details, and keeping others calm.
“The power just went out.” Requires working out what matters right now: light, fridge, medical devices, kids, phones.
“Gentler.” / “Faster.” / “Be more careful with that.” Requires adjusting its motion with no numeric target.
“Tell me when the laundry’s done.” Requires monitoring cues (sound, status light) and choosing when and how to notify.
“If it starts raining, close the windows.” Requires conditional rules that persist for days.
“Run the house while we’re away for a week.” Requires long-horizon autonomy, contingency handling, and knowing when to escalate.
“Learn the house.” Requires mapping rooms, objects, owners, no-go zones, shutoff locations, and the emergency plan, including in a home that isn’t yours.
“We’re on a call, be quiet.” Requires switching to a quiet mode and blocking noisy interruptions (doorbell, vacuum, notifications).
“Clean it without bleach — the baby’s crawling.” Requires substituting methods under a new constraint.
“Get ready for the storm / the plumber / the newborn.” Requires building an event-specific prep list from context.
“Calm the dog down.” Requires reading animal state (storm, fireworks, separation) and choosing a response.
“The dog’s limping.” Requires noticing and reporting without guessing at medical treatment.
